title: Leaders, Not Teams, Squander Leads
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Admired Leadership argues that complacency, not the team, is what loses a lead, and that blame for squandering an advantage belongs to the leader. The post says leads make teams lazy, defensive and unfocused, so leaders must ask for more precision and aggression when ahead. It treats a lead as a blanket of false security that lulls teams into lax execution. The author suggests playing a game within a game, measuring execution on a different metric, to prevent a protective posture. The closing advice is to act as if no advantage exists.
points: Protecting a lead is the fastest way to lose one, in sports and in business.
Leads make teams lazy and defensive, so the team is most vulnerable when ahead.
Losing a lead is a failure of leadership because leaders set the strategy the team executes.
Leaders should demand more precision, energy and offensive thinking when holding an edge.
A game within a game, measured by a different metric, helps keep complacency out.
quotes: Leads make teams lazy, defensive, and unfocused. Teams are the most vulnerable when they are ahead in any competition.

Leads are a blanket of false security that often lulls a team into lax execution. Once a team moves in slow motion and without the aggressive style that enabled the lead in the first place, any edge soon evaporates.
Losing a lead is a failure of leadership, not of the players or team members engaged in the contest. Leaders set the strategy and ask team members to execute.
With a lead or significant advantage, leaders must ask the team to be more, not less, precise with executing.
Leaders and coaches who are prepared for the lead challenge often ask the team to play a game within a game, whereby they measure successful execution using a different metric or indicator.
They never take a lead for granted. They keep the pressure on and act as if no advantage exists.
